trace.title: Scoped key
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Cache-aside reads a copy if present, otherwise loads from the authority and stores a copy.

The hard questions are which values may be stale, for how long, and how a write changes the cached answer.

Include tenant, query, and relevant version dimensions in keys. A TTL limits some stale lifetimes but does not prove immediate revocation or prevent old data being refilled after a race.

Permission-sensitive checks may need a fresh authority boundary separate from cached content.

When many keys expire together, requests can stampede the database. Use bounded rebuilds, jittered expiries, request coalescing, and stale-serving policies only where the product allows them.

A cache outage should not create unlimited fallback work.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Read miss → DB load → cache fill. Now interleave a write: A reads old DB, B commits new DB and deletes cache, A fills old value.

A simple “delete after write” rule can still have a stale-fill race.

Choose a consistency policy that matches the requirement: tolerate bounded staleness, version entries, use guarded refresh, or read the authority for strict decisions. Test the chosen timeline.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
TTL is not a universal correctness proof. Caching a denied/allowed result without proper context can leak access.

Cold-cache fallback can collapse the authority.
